text:
The cyberpunk metropolis, known in the archives as Neo-Veridia, was not merely a city but a living, breathing organism of steel and silicon. Its history was etched into the very foundations, laid during the Great Convergence of the late 21st century when corporate sovereignty superseded national borders. The skyscrapers, towering monoliths of reinforced glass and carbon nanotube composites, were not just architectural feats but symbols of the vertical stratification of society. The upper spires, bathed in the perpetual glow of the neon constellations, housed the elite and the corporate overlords, while the lower levels, perpetually shrouded in a smog of exhaust and steam, were the domain of the laborers and the disenfranchised.

The streets below were a chaotic symphony of motion and sound. Hovercars, sleek and silent, wove through the airways in complex, algorithmically optimized patterns, their underbellies casting shifting shadows on the wet pavement. The constant churn of humanity was a river of diverse faces, each carrying the weight of a world where technology had advanced faster than ethics. Omnipresent digital billboards, projected directly onto the retinas of citizens via neural links or displayed on massive holographic screens, pulsed with advertisements for synthetic emotions, memory wipes, and augmented limbs. These screens were the eyes of the city, watching, recording, and influencing every move, creating an atmosphere of both exhilarating freedom and suffocating surveillance.

In the midst of this high-tech dystopia, a single, anachronistic object sat on a rusted metal table in a dimly lit alleyway café: a candle. The primary material of this candle was beeswax, harvested from the last remaining natural hives in the off-world colonies. Unlike the paraffin and synthetic polymers that dominated the market, this beeswax retained a faint, sweet aroma of honey and earth, a sensory reminder of a natural world that had largely been replaced by the synthetic. The wax was pale gold, translucent in the flickering light, and its slow, steady burn provided a rare moment of quiet contemplation in a city that never slept.
